title: MCP 2026-07-28 Spec: Stateless Core & Extensions
content:
## Overview

On July 28, 2026, the Model Context Protocol project shipped the **2026-07-28 specification** — described as the most substantial revision to MCP since the introduction of authorization. The headline change: MCP's transport moves from a stateful, session-based model to a **stateless core**, with less-central features like Tasks split out into a formal extensions framework.

Adoption has scaled well past the early-days framing of "a promising standard." More than **10,000 public MCP servers** are running in production, the TypeScript and Python SDKs have each individually crossed **1 billion cumulative downloads**, and combined Tier 1 SDK downloads are approaching **half a billion per month**. OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, and AWS have all built MCP support into their own agent stacks, cementing it as the de facto tool-connection standard rather than an Anthropic-only convention.

---

## Stateless Transport

Prior MCP revisions pinned a client to a specific server process for the life of a session via the `Mcp-Session-Id` header. The 2026-07-28 spec removes protocol-level sessions entirely: any request can be served by any server instance behind ordinary HTTP load balancing, with no sticky routing required. This is the change that lets MCP servers run behind standard horizontally-scaled infrastructure instead of needing session-affinity hacks.

To replace what sessions used to provide, the spec adds:

- **Multi Round-Trip Requests** — a single logical operation can span several HTTP request/response pairs without a shared session object holding state between them
- **Header-based routing** — routing information that used to live in an implicit session now travels explicitly in request headers
- **Cacheable list results** — `tools/list`, `resources/list`, and similar calls can now be cached and reused across requests, cutting latency for clients that re-check available tools frequently

---

## Tasks Becomes an Extension

MCP's **Tasks** feature — used for tracking long-running operations that outlive a single request — is no longer part of the core protocol. It now ships as a versioned **extension**, part of a broader move to keep the protocol core small and let optional capabilities (Tasks, and the newer **Apps** extension) evolve independently without forcing a core spec bump every time.

---

## Authorization Hardening

The revision strengthens the authorization model with tighter **OAuth and OIDC** support, closing gaps that had made some MCP server implementations vulnerable to token confusion or replay issues under the previous session-based flow.

---

## Compatibility Warning

This is a breaking change: **servers built against 2026-07-28 are not guaranteed to work with pre-2026-07-28 clients, and vice versa.** Anyone running an MCP server or client in production should check which spec revision their SDK targets before upgrading, since the removal of `Mcp-Session-Id` and the Tasks extraction both change wire-level behavior, not just internals.

---

## Why It Matters

The practical effect for anyone building MCP servers (including the ones connected to Claude Code) is that servers become easier to deploy at scale — no session affinity, standard HTTP caching for list calls — at the cost of a migration for anything hand-rolled against the older stateful model. Given MCP's download and adoption numbers, this spec revision is effectively an infrastructure-wide upgrade for the agentic tooling ecosystem, not a niche protocol tweak.
